witness_rows.one_liner: relied on her arrangements, even after her stroke
witness_rows.summary: Weston said only Liston could arrange 'Spirit of Our Ancestors', told how he goaded her back to work after the stroke that left her unable to play, after which she learned to write music by computer with her left hand, and praised her genius and spiritual strength through years of illness.
witness_rows.lead_quote: Then I realized that only Melba Liston could do this.
witness_rows.caution: The stroke anecdote includes 'I insulted her as only musicians can do. I called her all kinds of names' and 'She cried a little bit' -- affectionate goading in context, but harsh if excerpted; avoid quoting those lines alone. Dates are Weston's recollection: he places the Hawkins Five Spot date in 1959 and the Montreal festival concert in 1985, while the interviewer dates the Montreal residency to '97 -- check against the discography. The interviewer's 'long partnership' phrase is hers, not his.

she_said.one_liner: arranged his music for 40 years

I think he pulled me out of it – helped anyway. I thank him very much for sticking with me, because nobody else did.

The quotes chosen are after that point. The claim that Hampton 'did stuff with Melba Liston' on trombone-choir records is the interviewer's (Brower), not confirmed by Hampton. witness_rows.one_liner: interviewed her for the smithsonian
witness_rows.summary: Bryant, interviewing Liston, praised her arranging (the shadings, the string voicings, 'My Reverie' as one of the most beautiful things she had done), her trombone sound and her resilience after her stroke, and told her she had admired her from afar for years, had lately become bonded to her, and counted her a guiding light for many women, Bryant included.
witness_rows.lead_quote: you have been the best, Melba. You’ve been a guiding light for a lot of people, including me
witness_rows.caution: Bryant is the interviewer: her lines are addressed to Liston in the second person, and many are leading questions or hearsay that Liston did not confirm or corrected -- e.g. Gerald Wilson's claim that Liston recorded with Basie (Liston did not remember it), 'how you got the school systems down there' (Liston: 'I didn't get the school systems'), the Pittsburgh Jazz Orchestra/Harlem Backstreet/Pratt Institute list (Bryant says 'I'd never heard of these', i.e. read from a source), the Ellington-influence suggestion (Liston: 'I do it all from my soul'), and the State Department 'it's been said' reports. Do not present these as established facts. Bracketed passages in her blocks are transcriber summaries, not her words. 'Maybe in the last year we became bonded' means their close friendship was recent; the long admiration was 'from afar'. Second quote is about 'My Reverie' -- name the piece when displaying.
witness_rows.doc_title: Melba Liston — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

witness_rows.one_liner: held her up as a rare exception
witness_rows.summary: Lincoln, dismissing the idea of a women's history in jazz, singled Liston out as the rare woman who comes to the music for the music.

she_said.summary: Looking at a photograph of her youth band from about 1938, Liston said she knew everyone in it except the drummer and a tall saxophonist, and named Minnie, whose surname the transcriber could only guess.
she_said.her_quote: Everybody except the drummer, and I don’t know who the tall saxophonist is, but the rest of them I know. That’s me. Minnie – Minnie

she_said.one_liner: recognised him in her youth-band photograph
she_said.summary: Bryant pointed out Prince Harris in a photograph of Liston's youth band from about 1938, and Liston recognised him.
she_said.her_quote: Yeah, there’s Prince.
she_said.bryant_quote: Prince Harris.

she_said.one_liner: pictured with her childhood circle
she_said.summary: According to the transcriber's summaries, Liston thought an unidentified man in an early photograph was Robert Ross, Bryant produced another photograph showing Ross, and Ross appears with Minnie and Alice in a third photograph.

she_said.one_liner: named among the promising women players
she_said.summary: Liston raised 'a drummer' among the promising women musicians, Bryant supplied the name Teri Lyne Carrington, and Liston agreed, adding that they had to go back East.
she_said.her_quote: And who else? I know they got to get out and go back East.
she_said.bryant_quote: Teri Lyne Carrington?

she_said.one_liner: her aunt, who danced to the player piano
she_said.summary: Liston said her aunties would dance while she pedalled the player piano, and agreed when Bryant asked whether Thelma did too.
she_said.her_quote: Yeah, and my aunties would dance.
she_said.bryant_quote: Thelma too?

she_said.summary: A transcriber's summary of Bryant's prompts lists Vernon Slater among the bandmembers who moved with Liston from Bardu Ali's band to Gerald Wilson's.

she_said.one_liner: her grandmother
she_said.summary: Liston's grandmother, named Virginia by the transcriber, moved to California with Liston's aunts some months before Liston and her mother followed.
she_said.her_quote: My mom and me stayed over, and my grandma and my aunties moved out here.

witness_rows.one_liner: cited her among jazz's early women players
witness_rows.summary: Freeman cited Liston on trombone as one of the few early women in jazz, who he said had to be 'great, great, great, great' before men would accept them.
witness_rows.lead_quote: And then Melba [Liston] plays the trombone.
witness_rows.caution: Freeman says only 'Melba'; the surname '[Liston]' is a Smithsonian editorial bracket (identification is very likely). The second quote is about women generally, not Liston specifically. Block 271162 is the interviewer's question.
